A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Tchebycheff set scalarization work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated results.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on convex many-objective optimization and noisy mixed linear and nonlinear regression, including results over 50 runs in the main text and Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds author-trained CelebA models, parameter sensitivity experiments, and runtime measurements. It distinguishes its CelebA results from comparator scores taken from prior work.

M1.justification: The TCH-Set and STCH-Set objectives, smoothing formulations, and gradient update in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. V2 newly documents and tests smoothing schedules, but does not establish that these replace a different procedure used in v1. Applying the method to CelebA does not introduce a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: V2 adds real-data deep multi-task grouping on nine CelebA attribute-classification tasks, extending coverage beyond v1's synthetic convex optimization and mixed regression problems. All original synthetic coverage, including 1,024-objective optimization and the regression noise levels, remains.

E2.justification: V2 Table 4 introduces Random Grouping, HOA, TAG, and DMTG as actual comparators for CelebA, using scores attributed to Gao et al. (2024). HOA and TAG were previously cited but not included in reported comparisons. The original synthetic comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include training two, three, or four ResNet-variant models on CelebA with cross-entropy and Adam for 100 epochs, evaluating task-level classification performance, comparing fixed and adaptive smoothing, sampling Dirichlet preferences, and measuring runtime. These extend the evaluation design; the original synthetic dimensions, sample counts, noise levels, and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests smoothing sensitivity with five fixed values versus an adaptive schedule, preference sensitivity with several Dirichlet distributions versus uniform weights, and runtime scalability across objective counts. These investigate optimization choices and computational behavior beyond the retained solution-count and noise-level comparisons.

E5.justification: The original experiments retain 50 independent runs, mean reporting, and Wilcoxon rank-sum comparisons at the 0.05 level. The added CelebA, sensitivity, and runtime results do not introduce new seed disclosures, uncertainty intervals, repeated-run specifications, or statistical testing procedures.

E6.justification: The original synthetic numerical results are unchanged, including v1 Table 1 retained in v2 Table 6 and v1 Tables 4–5 retained as Tables 7–8. V2 adds substantial new results: Table 4 reports a worst-task score of 11.89 for STCH-Set versus 12.18 for DMTG at K=2, while SoM has the better average, 5.80 versus 5.81. Tables 9–11 add sensitivity findings and runtimes, including 58 seconds for STCH-Set versus 5,500 seconds for MosT at 128 objectives.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes from guaranteeing weak Pareto optimality for every member of an optimal TCH-Set set to asserting existence of an optimal set composed of Pareto-optimal solutions; the unique-set guarantee remains. Appendix A.1 replaces the corresponding proof. V2 also explicitly states nonredundancy and positive-preference assumptions and adds Appendix A.5's counterexample discussion and guarantee comparison.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a small complementary solution set, TCH-Set and its smooth variant, efficient optimization, and theoretical and experimental support. The precise theoretical guarantee changes in the body, but these headline contribution claims are not substantively rewritten.

C2.justification: V2 explains the weaker guarantee for nonsmooth TCH-Set and contrasts it with STCH-Set. Appendix D adds interpretations involving smoothing and optimization landscapes, hard versus smooth clustering, preference-dependent objectives, computational scaling, and budget-dependent solution counts. The original limitation to fully observable deterministic objectives and the nonlinear-regression failure discussion remain.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation documentation: Appendix B.4 specifies CelebA tasks, backbone family, loss, optimizer, learning rate, decay, training duration, and the borrowed implementation source. Appendix D documents shared smoothing parameters, an annealing formula, and preference choices. The authors' own code remains promised upon publication. The annealing formula and stated endpoint are internally inconsistent.

R1.justification: V2 adds context on strong linear scalarization, smooth scalarization in multitask and reinforcement learning, DMTG, homotopy optimization, and weighted clustering. These broaden supporting connections while retaining the central positioning relative to SoM, MosT, and Pareto-front approximation. Publication-status updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact. Changes include localized explanatory rewrites around assumptions and guarantees, additional cross-references and appendix organization, author-contact edits, and conversion to author-year citations. Table 3's caption is corrected from linear to nonlinear regression.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document template and typography, refreshes early illustrations, and adds Figure 4 plus Tables 4, 5, and 9–11. The full convex-results table moves to Appendix C as Table 6, while a shortened version remains as Table 1. These substantially change the displays and presentation beyond renumbering or numerical edits.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's synthetic-only empirical support through CelebA evaluation and targeted sensitivity and runtime evidence. It also withdraws the overbroad universal TCH-Set guarantee and explains the weaker claim. These address important weaknesses in validation and theoretical qualification. The repair is incomplete: Appendix A.5's example does not establish strict domination and makes its second solution redundant, while Appendix D.1's smoothing formula conflicts with its stated endpoint. Those defects limit theoretical rigor and reproducibility, but the added validation and more cautious guarantee still provide a substantial overall gain.
